body.x: Making a Move in the Next-Generation TV Market with the OLED TV

The display of your dreams, it’s called. OLED (organic light-emitting diode) TVs are on the verge of going on a worldwide rampage. As the OLED TV is able to emit its own light and color, no separate light source is necessary, which enables the screen design to be thin and light. In addition, OLED TVs have a wider angle of vision and a faster response time than the LCD TVs which are currently the mainstream product on the market. OLED offers clear resolution with no afterimage even in shows with fast moving-images such as action movies and sports matches. For these reasons, the market scale of OLED TVs could quite possibly grow fast enough to challenge LCD TVs in only a few years. According to a forecast by global market research firm DisplaySearch, the OLED TV market will grow by more than 10 times each year through 2014, giving it more than 10 million yearly sales by 2016.

Even counting LG Electronics, there are barely a handful of players that can put OLED TVs into mass production, and they are all locked in a furious battle to spread awareness of the excellence of their respective products. This reflects just how important it is to be the first to seize the market and gain the ascendency, and it is also the reason that LG Electronics is giving the OLED TV so much display space at the KES 2012 and a variety of other expositions around the world.

LG Electronics’ OLED TV (55EM9700) is based on WRGB OLED technology. The company hopes to make its set stand above the rest with rich and accurate color reproduction through 4-color pixels, wide-angle vision based on color refiner technology, infinite dynamic contrast range, a screen with fast response speed and no after images, and super-slim/super-lightweight design.

And the TV certainly is thin – the 4mm design is thinner than your typical smartphone, and indeed it is the thinnest TV on the market today. By replacing the aluminum on the back with the new high-strength, high-elasticity material known as CFRP (carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer), LG has brought the weight down to an astonishingly light 10kg.
Don’t Forget the UD TV Market

Unlike its competitors, LG Electronics is also getting actively involved in the production of UD (ultra-high-definition) TVs. UD TVs are divided into 4K and 8K according to their resolution, which means that they are either four times (4,096x2,160 or 3,840x2,160) or 8 times (7,680x4,320) higher than full HD (high definition) resolution (1,920x1,080). One advance that UD TVs have over OLED is that they can be made larger with less difficulty.

The UD TV that LG Electronics has just released (84LM9600) is an 84-inch TV – the largest TV ever to be launched in Korea. With 4K resolution (3,840x2,160), it has brought life-like realism to new heights. The pixels are packed together so tightly that you can’t see the rectangular pixel lines, and the crystal-clear images impacting your retinas make you feel like you’re actually in the show instead of just watching it.

Applying high-resolution data processing technology, LG Electronics has equipped its Cinema3D UD Engine to achieve lossless depiction of ultra-high-definition images. The device can even upgrade ordinary programs so the clarity and fluidity of UD resolution.

The TV delivers unbelievable 3D stereophonic sound through the deluxe 2.2 channel sound system equipped with two stereo speakers and two woofers. All this is presented in luxurious monochrome platinum-like material.

This product also shows off LG’s unique Cinema3D technology, featuring glasses that are light as a feather and easy on the eyes. Later, LG is planning on releasing a variety of UD programs through the LG Smart TV including Story Book, which matches carefully selected masterpieces of literature with classical music.
